facts.statement: The study tested the cyanobacteria-derived compound barbamide and related molecules to see how they affect sensory nerve cells.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: The first tests used a multi-electrode setup to measure electrical activity in pain-sensing cells grown from human stem cells.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: All three tested compounds lowered the rate at which these cells fired electrical signals, with stronger effects at higher doses, suggesting they could act as pain relievers.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: To understand how the compound works, researchers used a technique called whole-cell patch clamp on human sensory nerve cells.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Barbamide reduced both spontaneous and triggered electrical signals in the human nerve cells without causing obvious cell damage.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: The team also checked whether barbamide affects the growth of nerve extensions in PC12 cells and mouse nerve tissue.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: Barbamide and a modified version of it increased the growth of nerve extensions in the tested cells.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue
